newsitem.title: HUNGARY: BT enters Hungary telecoms, sees growth.
newsitem.headline: BT enters Hungary telecoms, sees growth.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc (BT) said on Thursday it was entering the telecommunications business in Hungary and planned to expand its presence as the sector was gradually deregulated.

"Over time, we will be in domestic services in Hungary and other countries...as long as we can make some money out of it and it is a sensible commercial thing to do," Mark Smith, BT's General Manager for southern and eastern Europe, told a news conference in Budapest.
Earlier in London BT said it had appointed GTS Hungary, a subsidiary of U.S.-based Global TeleSystems Group Inc, as its distributor of Concert services in Hungary.
The Concert package, including Concert Frame Relay Services, is a business communications facility offered mainly to multinational companies, a GTS official said.
"GTS expects a $500,000 turnover on Concert services for next year," said Robert Horvath, head of GTS Hungary.
BT regards GTS as more than just a partner in Hungary, as GTS also distributes Concert in the Czech Republic, Smith said, adding that the cooperation could expand further.
Both companies refused to say how the profits will be shared between them.
Smith said BT is not overly concerned about increasing competition in Hungary's telecommunications market.
"The fact that there are already so many competitors shows that we are in the right marketplace," he said.
Concert is a joint venture 75 percent owned by BT and 25 percent by U.S's MCI Communications Corp, established in 1993 with an $1 billion capital.
BT also owns a 20 percent stake in MCI worth $4.3 billion.
Presently data transfer services and telecomm hardware are the areas where large companies like Siemens and Ericsson compete in Hungary.
Matav, 67 percent owned by a 50-50 consortium of Deutsche Telekom AG and Ameritech Corp, has a concession giving it monopoly on terrestrial communications until 22 December 2001.

The OECD, which admitted Hungary as a member in March, recommended in April that Hungary's government should renegotiate the existing concession with Matav, considering that the EU market will be deregulated in 1998.
